title: Tokyo Hired People to Shove You Onto Trains #shorts

lines.text: What if your job was shoving people onto a train?
In Tokyo, that job is real!
trains carried more than twice the people they were built for.
Mostly students, in neat uniforms and bright white gloves.
They pushed backs, shoulders and bags, until everyone fit.
Then the doors closed, and the train left right on time.
Long before Tokyo, New York subway guards shoved crowds onto trains too!
So next time your train feels packed, just be glad nobody's paid to push you.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Passenger pusher': first brought in at Shinjuku Station as 'passenger arrangement staff', largely part-time students; 1964 LIFE described 'white-gloved official pushers'; in 1975 rush-hour trains averaged 221% of designed capacity; still used on some of the most crowded Tokyo lines

Wikipedia, 'Passenger pusher' (New York): a 1918 New York Times article describes subway guards and police pushing crowds onto trains on the 42nd Street Shuttle; by the 1920s subway pushers were known as 'sardine packers'
JRPass blog, 'Oshiya: The True Story of Japan's Train Pushers' (busiest from the 1960s to the 1980s; part-time students at the busiest stations)
